@paleface and @gbj1301 have excellent advice. Linux is just safer.

  • If you run Linux, you should never be installing software from untrusted websites or email attachments. Like Apple's app store, a Linux distro's repository should be well-vetted and safe.

  • If you inadvertently download something bad, your download folder should already be configured to disallow program execution (malware can't auto-execute / auto-install as it can and does on Windows).

  • And even if the first two controls don't stop malware, any *nix OS will still force you the end-user to provide superuser credentials before the software can install (as long as you aren't running as root or another superuser). An unexpected request for superuser credentials should should serve as a warning for most users that something important is happening. This is default behavior. From your $HOME directory, type the following:

$ ls -l Downloads

The permissions for the files in that folder should look something like this: -rw-r-----. Since this is your user home and you are the owner of the files in question, you have read/write privileges, but not execution. You can open a file with an external program (read) and make/save changes to the file (write) but the file cannot run (execute) on its own.
